The formal CLT establishes a convergence in distribution to a standard normal variable, showing how the distribution of errors around the mean behaves. This is then illustrated with an example of waiting times where the individual asymmetry disappears when averaging 100 observations.


The sample proportion is the average of zeros and ones; by the CLT, it's approximately normal, forming the basis for error margins. Formally, given Bernoulli distributed variables, the sample proportion converges in distribution to a normal distribution with mean p and variance p(1-p)/n. This enables constructing confidence intervals, replacing the unknown true proportion with its sample estimate using Slutsky's theorem. The margin of error decreases with the square root of the sample size.

An electoral poll example with 400 respondents, where 55% support candidate A, results in a 95% confidence interval for the true proportion.

The Continuous Mapping Theorem (CMT) states that if an estimator is consistent, any continuous function of it is consistent for the same function of the parameter. The probability limit of a function applied to a converging variable is equivalent to the function of the probability limit. Unlike expected values, the probability limit goes through nonlinear functions.


The sample variance converging in probability to the population variance implies the sample standard deviation consistently estimates the population standard deviation. A similar logic applies to the inverse of the sample mean, under the condition that the population mean is not zero. Considering the F-distribution relationship with t-distribution and its convergence to the Chi-squared distribution is crucial.

Slutsky's theorem is fundamental: if one sequence converges in distribution and another converges in probability to a constant, they can be combined by treating the second as the constant, enabling parameter substitution with consistent estimators. Applying Slutsky's Theorem, the t-statistic converges in distribution to a standard normal distribution because the unknown population standard deviation can be replaced by the consistent estimator, sample standard deviation. This allows use of the normal distribution even when population variance is unknown, and data is not necessarily normal.


The Delta Method extends the concept of consistency; if an estimator is approximately normal, a smooth function of it is also approximately normal, along with its asymptotic standard error. The formal expression and the first-order Taylor expansion provide the basis for this approximation. An example demonstrating the calculation of the standard error of a transformed estimator using the Delta Method, specifically estimating the reciprocal of the sample mean, illustrates its practical application.
